title: Hypertension
description: Long-term high blood pressure in the arteries
wiki_lead:
Hypertension, also known as high blood pressure, is a long-term medical condition in which the blood pressure in the arteries is persistently elevated. High blood pressure usually does not cause symptoms itself. It is, however, a major risk factor for stroke, coronary artery disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, peripheral arterial disease, vision loss, chronic kidney disease, and dementia. Hypertension is a major cause of premature death worldwide.
High blood pressure is classified as primary (essential) hypertension or secondary hypertension. About 90–95% of cases are primary, defined as high blood pressure due to non-specific lifestyle and genetic factors. Lifestyle factors that increase the risk include excess salt in the diet, excess body weight, smoking, physical inactivity, and alcohol use. The remaining 5–10% of cases are categorized as secondary hypertension, defined as high blood pressure due to a clearly identifiable cause, such as chronic kidney disease, narrowing of the kidney arteries, an endocrine disorder, or the use of birth control pills.
Blood pressure is classified by two measurements, the systolic (first number) and diastolic (second number) pressures. For most adults, normal blood pressure at rest is under 120 millimeters mercury (mmHg) systolic and 80 mmHg diastolic, elevated blood pressure is between 120 and 129 mmHg systolic and under 80 mmHg diastolic and high blood pressure is present if the resting blood pressure is persistently at or above 130/80 (stage 1) or 140/90 (stage 2) mmHg. Different numbers apply to children. Ambulatory blood pressure monitoring over a 24-hour period appears more accurate than office-based blood pressure measurement.
Lifestyle changes and medications can lower blood pressure and decrease the risk of health complications. Lifestyle changes include weight loss, physical exercise, decreased salt intake, reducing alcohol intake, and a healthy diet. If lifestyle changes are not sufficient, blood pressure medications are used. Up to three medications taken concurrently can control blood pressure in 90% of people. The treatment of moderately high arterial blood pressure (defined as >160/100 mmHg) with medications is associated with an improved life expectancy. The effect of treatment of blood pressure between 130/80 mmHg and 160/100 mmHg is less clear, with some reviews finding benefit and others finding unclear or no benefit. High blood pressure affects 33% of the population globally. About half of all people with high blood pressure do not know that they have it. In 2019, high blood pressure was believed to have been a factor in 19% of all deaths (10.4 million globally).

Signs and symptoms
Hypertension is rarely accompanied by symptoms. Half of all people with hypertension are unaware that they have it. Hypertension is usually identified as part of health screening or when seeking healthcare for an unrelated problem.
Some people with high blood pressure report headaches, as well as lightheadedness, vertigo, tinnitus (buzzing or hissing in the ears), altered vision or fainting episodes. These symptoms, however, might be related to associated anxiety rather than the high blood pressure itself.
Long-standing untreated hypertension can cause organ damage with signs such as changes in the optic fundus seen by ophthalmoscopy. The severity of hypertensive retinopathy correlates roughly with the duration or the severity of the hypertension. Other hypertension-caused organ damage include chronic kidney disease and thickening of the heart muscle.


Secondary hypertension

Secondary hypertension is hypertension due to an identifiable cause and may result in certain specific additional signs and symptoms. For example, as well as causing high blood pressure, Cushing's syndrome frequently causes truncal obesity, glucose intolerance, moon face, a hump of fat behind the neck and shoulders (referred to as a buffalo hump), and purple abdominal stretch marks. grok_lead: Hypertension, commonly known as high blood pressure, is a chronic medical condition characterized by persistently elevated pressure in the arteries, which forces the heart to work harder to pump blood throughout the body. Per the 2025 ACC/AHA guidelines, hypertension is staged as follows: Stage 1: Systolic 130â139 mm Hg or diastolic 80â89 mm Hg Stage 2: Systolic â¥140 mm Hg or diastolic â¥90 mm Hg (Note: some international standards, like those from the World Health Organization, use a threshold of 140/90 mm Hg or higher.) Treatment decisions may vary by stage, risk factors, and comorbidities, with lifestyle interventions recommended initially for stage 1 in lower-risk individuals. This condition affects the cardiovascular system primarily but can lead to widespread organ damage, particularly to the heart, brain, and kidneys, if uncontrolled. Globally, hypertension affects approximately 1.4 billion adults aged 30â79 years (about one in three in this age group), with more than two-thirds residing in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs). Awareness is low, with nearly half unaware globally, and control rates in LMICs are poor (around 10% in some studies). Hypertension is known as the "silent killer" because it is often asymptomatic until severe complications occur and is a major cause of premature death worldwide. The WHO's 2023 open access global report on hypertension emphasizes that effective treatment could prevent millions of deaths, strokes, and heart attacks between 2023 and 2050. In the United States, nearly half of all adultsâabout 120 million peopleâhave hypertension, though many remain unaware or untreated, contributing to its status as a major public health challenge. The condition is classified into two main types: primary ( essential) hypertension, which accounts for about 90â95% of cases and develops gradually without a specific identifiable cause, often linked to genetic and environmental factors; and secondary hypertension, which arises suddenly from underlying conditions such as kidney disease, adrenal gland disorders, or certain medications. Key risk factors for hypertension include non-modifiable elements like advancing age (prevalence rises to over 70% in those aged 60 and older), family history, and race (higher rates among Black individuals), as well as modifiable lifestyle factors such as obesity, physical inactivity, high sodium intake, diets high in saturated fats (e.g., butter, processed meats, fatty meats), high intake of simple sugars and processed products, excessive alcohol consumption, tobacco use, and chronic stress. Acute stress and anger can cause temporary spikes in blood pressure, while chronic or repeated stress or anger may contribute to long-term hypertension through repeated elevations. Similarly, excessive caffeine intake can cause temporary spikes in blood pressure. High carbohydrate/sugar intake is not a direct cause of blood pressure elevation in major sources but may contribute indirectly via obesity, insulin resistance, or metabolic syndrome. Although family history indicates genetic predisposition, with heritability estimates for blood pressure typically ranging from 30% to 60%, hypertension is multifactorial and genetic influences are not deterministic. Healthy lifestyle choicesâsuch as a low-sodium heart-healthy diet low in saturated fats and added sugars (e.g., DASH), regular physical activity, maintaining a healthy weight, avoiding smoking, limiting alcohol, managing stress, and ensuring good sleepâcan significantly mitigate genetic risk, allowing some individuals with a family history of hypertension to maintain low or optimal blood pressure. Pathophysiologically, it involves mechanisms like increased peripheral vascular resistance, overactivation of the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, and heightened sympathetic nervous activity, which elevate arterial pressure over time. Most individuals experience no symptoms, earning it the moniker "silent killer," but severe or prolonged cases may present with severe headaches, nosebleeds, fatigue, vision problems, chest pain, difficulty breathing, or irregular heartbeat. Untreated hypertension significantly increases the risk of serious complications, including heart attack, stroke, heart failure, kidney damage, aortic aneurysm, vision loss, and cognitive impairments like dementia. Diagnosis involves repeated blood pressure measurements, often confirmed on separate occasions, with classifications ranging from elevated (120â129/<80 mm Hg) to stage 2 hypertension (â¥140/â¥90 mm Hg) or hypertensive crisis (>180/>120 mm Hg, requiring immediate medical attention). Management focuses on lifestyle modificationsâsuch as adopting a low-sodium DASH diet, engaging in at least 150 minutes of moderate aerobic exercise weekly, maintaining a healthy weight, and quitting smoking âcombined with medications like diuretics, ACE inhibitors, or beta-blockers for those needing pharmacological intervention. Timely treatment is essential to prevent complications. Effective control can reduce cardiovascular risks by up to 30â40%, underscoring the importance of regular screening and early intervention.
